item.title: Assad officer extradited to Syria on war crimes charges for first time
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgjdy8q766o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Assad officer extradited to Syria on war crimes charges for first time - Published Lebanon has handed Syria a former general who served under the ousted regime of Bashar al-Assad, in the first extradition of its kind since his government fell. Maj Gen Adel Issa, 67, is accused of a raft of crimes allegedly committed during the Syrian civil war, which ended in December 2024 when rebel forces took the capital, Damascus, and Assad fled. Issa was detained on 8 August after visiting the Syrian embassy in Beirut to complete paperwork and was transferred into Syrian custody on Wednesday. The handover follows pressure from Syria's new authorities on Lebanon to act against former security and military officials who fled across the border after Assad's fall. The Syrian interior ministry said Issa led ground forces in the eastern province of Deir Ezzor until 2016. He is accused of charges including murder as well as "torture leading to death and crimes of aggression with the aim of inciting civil war and sectarian fighting", it said. Judicial officials told the BBC that Issa denied the charges during his arrest. The decision to extradite him was made under an agreement between the two countries dating back to 1951. Issa's case will now go before a referral judge in Damascus, who will decide whether it should proceed to a criminal court. In January, Syria gave Lebanese officials a list of more than 200 former senior officers it wants prosecuted. Since taking power, authorities led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa have pursued cases against dozens of former officials. Earlier this month, a Damascus court sentenced Assad and his brother, Maher, to death in absentia over abuses committed during the civil war. They fled to Moscow when Sharaa's forces seized power. Their cousins, Waseem al-Assad and Atif Najib, have been arrested in Syria and also sentenced to death. Additional reporting by BBC Arabic's Joya Berbery in Beirut

item.title: Founder of collapsed Chinese property giant Evergrande sentenced to life in prison
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd0x9mjjmgjo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Founder of collapsed Chinese property giant Evergrande sentenced to life in prison - Published The founder of Evergrande, the property giant at the centre of China's housing market slump, has been sentenced to life in prison and had all of his personal property confiscated. Hui Ka Yan pleaded guilty in April to several charges, including embezzlement of assets and corporate bribery. Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court also fined his former companies a total of 15.82bn yuan (£1.73bn; $2.35bn) over multiple crimes, including falsifying records and concealing debt. Hui's sentencing marks a key moment in the fallout from Evergrande's collapse, which shook China's property sector and hit investors and domestic banks hard. Hui and his businesses "seriously disrupted" the Chinese property market, resulting in significant economic losses, the court said. Other Evergrande executives, including Hui's two sons Xu Zhijian and Xu Tenghe, were also sentenced to jail terms ranging from 22 months to 18 years, according to state media. Once ranked Asia's richest man, Hui has seen his wealth and influence dwindle as his company unravelled. Hui, also known as Xu Jiayin, rose from humble beginnings in rural China, where he was raised by his grandmother before venturing into property development and setting up Evergrande in 1996. He oversaw the company's rapid rise through an aggressive expansion programme funded with large amounts of borrowed money. Evergrande became China's biggest real estate developer, with a stock market valuation of more than $50bn (£36.7bn). Hui was once estimated to be Asia's richest person. - Evergrande: Why should I care about the crisis-hit Chinese property giant? - Published25 August 2025 - Anxious Chinese home buyers reel from Evergrande crisis - Published29 September 2023 - Crisis-hit China Evergrande ordered to liquidate - Published29 January 2024 The firm was dealt a huge blow when Beijing introduced measures in 2020 to control debt in the country's property sector. As the company struggled to meet interest payments on its debts it sold properties at huge discounts to stay afloat before collapsing in 2021. In April, the court heard that the company had taken millions of dollars in pre-sale funding from potential house buyers that were not used for construction. The money had instead been channelled to new property developments, resulting in hundreds of unfinished projects. In March 2024, Hui was fined $6.5m and banned from China's capital market for life for his company overstating its revenue by $78bn. Evergrande's stock market valuation shrank by 99% before its shares were removed from the Hong Kong exchange in August 2025 after more than a decade and a half of trading. Evergrande's implosion has often been blamed for triggering a broader slump in China's property market that continues to weigh heavily on the economy. At its height, Evergrande was the biggest firm in the country's real estate industry, which made up about a third of China's gross domestic product at the time. The property market was a significant driver of growth and an important revenue source for local governments. The industry's ongoing problems have weighed heavily on the world's second largest economy as several other major developers faced financial woes.

item.title: Fix schools, say India's 'cockroach' protesters. Schoolchildren agree
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckg4q8kyxp7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Fix schools, say India's 'cockroach' protesters. Schoolchildren agree - Published The squat one-storey building has recently received a fresh coat of paint and looks respectable from a distance. But this government-run primary school for girls in Faridabad, a district on the outskirts of the Indian capital Delhi, suffers from a host of problems. The road outside the school in Khedi Kalan village is dotted with shallow potholes filled with filthy water. Inside, local social worker Satpal Narwat points out the plaster falling from the ceiling. "It looks new from the outside, but it's crumbling from inside. Four of its eight toilets are unusable and full of trash, while four of the nine classrooms have also been abandoned because they are too unsafe for children," he says, adding that in the rains, "the classrooms get flooded and children have no place to sit". This is not an isolated case. Many schools, especially in rural India, are starved of funding and in disrepair. India spends only 4.1% of its GDP on education. While this meets Unesco's lower minimum threshold of 4%, several countries - including France, Germany, Australia, Brazil and the US - spend more than 5% of their GDP on education. Countries like Belgium and Sweden spend even more. Experts - and the Indian government's own National Education Policy (NEP) - have recommended 6% as the ideal mark for India. According to official data, 94,000 government schools have closed here between 2014-15 and 2024-25. A report, external by government think-tank Niti Aayog says some were merged as part of efforts to streamline the system, but acknowledges that enrolment has fallen as demand for private schools has risen. The poor state of government schools is the focus of a new campaign by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). The online satirical movement made global headlines for its weeks-long protest in Delhi, which culminated in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan last month. The protests had erupted in May after NEET, India's biggest medical entrance exam, was cancelled following a question paper leak, forcing nearly two million students to retake the test. More than 20 students died by suicide, with their families blaming the scandal. Named #SchoolThikKaro (#FixTheSchool), the CJP's latest campaign is aimed at highlighting the crumbling infrastructure in government schools and pressuring authorities into addressing it. "Government schools, especially in rural India, have been neglected for many many decades now. So, children who grow up in villages don't have equal opportunities and they end up working in farms or as a daily wage labourer or construction workers," CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke told the BBC. "It's only because they don't get the same facilities and the same opportunities that children in big cities get. And that is what we are trying to change by making schools better." On Thursday, Dipke said he had visited more than 20 rural schools and had "not found even a single good school". "There were no benches, no bathrooms, no drinking water, no facilities at all. Even animals would not be kept in such a place," he said. "What I saw was really heartbreaking. This is very similar to what I used to see when I used to visit my village during school summer vacation. And even after 20 years, nothing have changed there." In recent days, Dipke and other CJP leaders have shared several videos - of leaking roofs, dirty toilets, children sitting on the floor and angry students - with their 26 million Instagram followers. "We want to ensure that children get benches to sit on, good washrooms and clean drinking water. They should have smart classrooms with digital boards. That is when they will also feel that they are getting the same quality of education as those living in big cities in the country," Dipke said. The government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi or his Bharatiya Janata Party have not commented on the campaign. The BBC has also contacted India's education ministry for a response. Meanwhile, the CJP's protest in Delhi and the campaign to fix schools appear to have emboldened students across India and opened floodgates of complaints and set off localised mutinies against an administration many accuse of being apathetic. Armed with mobile phones, school students have been shooting and posting videos on social media - some of which have gone viral and prompted authorities to act. After one video, external of schoolgirls in Raigad, Maharashtra, mocking the condition of the road leading to their school went viral, the local authorities repaired it In Uttar Pradesh, another video showed students running into the district magistrate's office demanding a road to their school, while a third , externalshowed schoolgirls asking an official whether he would send his own children to a school in such poor condition. At Delhi's Jantar Mantar, where the CJP held its earlier protest, the group demanded Pradhan's resignation as well as an overhaul of India's education system with greater accountability. Journalist and author Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay says "by the end of their protest, it was clear that it wasn't just about one exam or one minister's resignation". "People there were talking about the state of schools and everything that's wrong with them." Mukhopadhyay says the #FixTheSchool campaign is an obvious next step and "the way people have contributed with videos, pointing out flaws in school infrastructure, is evidence that the movement is gaining ground". "It can't be Jantar Mantar 2.0 as it will be much slower and a long-lasting movement. But the CJP will get a lot of support for the campaign because there's plenty to talk about that's wrong with the schools," he adds. One of the biggest problems government schools face is a lack of teachers and other staff, says Chatar Singh, treasurer of the Primary Teachers' Association in Haryana state where Faridabad is located. Singh is also the head teacher of the primary school in Atmadpur village. Its new building, funded by a private company's corporate social responsibility programme, and students' trophies make it one of the better-equipped schools in the area. But as we approach the toilets near the school gate, a stench greets me. Singh says the toilets have not been cleaned properly for the past two days because the part-time cleaner - appointed by the government to come in for a couple of hours every morning - has been sick. But dirty toilets are not his biggest problem – it is the lack of teachers, he says. For the school's 910 children, there are 40 teachers. But on Wednesday when BBC visited the institution, 30 had been deployed to help with voters' list revision, four others were off sick, leaving only six teachers to manage the children. "Teachers are hired to teach, but across India, government deploys them to do a lot of non-teaching assignments. They are used for election duty and to conduct Census. Most of my teachers have been on voters' list revision duty since July. It's affecting the quality of education," he says. Asked why he thinks the government schools are neglected, Singh says, "Do children of bureaucrats and MPs and politicians study in my school? No. They send their children to private schools because they can afford them." Most students here are children of migrant factory labourers, he says. "And a majority of them are from underprivileged castes and communities. Anyone who can afford sends their children to private school," he adds. His claim holds true across India. It is visible in the mushrooming of private schools in small towns and villages. In Khedi Kalan when he was growing up, Narwat says, there were only government schools near him and he got his education there. The crumbling girls' primary school which he gave me a tour of upsets him because the 62-year-old studied here from 1968 to 1973. "In those days, this was the only school in the village for both boys and girls," he says. "The school building was relatively new. There were eight rooms and all were filled with students." He says flooding became a serious problem after the road outside was raised about 15 years ago, leaving the school below road level. Narwat, who retired as an officer in the state's electricity office two years back, says he sent his children to the same school, but later moved them to a private school because they have better facilities. Narwat then takes us to the second primary school in the village - this one for boys, just a couple of hundred metres away. Here, classes are operating out of two rooms and a veranda. A second building with three classrooms was declared "condemned" and demolished about five years ago with assurance that a better one would be rebuilt. The patch is now a parking stand for cycles. Over the years, Narwat has petitioned chief minister, MPs and district officials, and written to the National Human Rights Commission, seeking improvements to the two Khedi Kalan schools. But he says little has changed. "I send my grandchildren to a private school," he says. "It's very expensive, but they have all the facilities. In village schools, the teachers are on election duty, and there's no library or laboratory." The CJP campaign has given him some hope that the schools will finally get attention. "I think the CJP can be a force for good. They've taught people to fight, to not be afraid. The government has all the power and resources. And now they have to perform."

item.title: Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj364klz857o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction - Published Once the undisputed giant of Nigerian politics, the Peoples Democratic Party now finds itself on the brink of extinction. A question hanging over the campaign for January's general election, which officially kicked off this week, is whether the PDP can survive. A factional struggle that has ended up in the courts over who exactly is in charge could end up rendering it irrelevant at the ballot box. It is a remarkable fall for the party, founded in 1998, which appeared impregnable after the end of military rule a year later - so much so that its chairman boasted in 2008 that it would govern for six decades. For 16 years, it controlled the presidency - in the shape of Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and then Goodluck Jonathan - and the vast majority of the country's 36 states. But the 2015 federal election was a seismic shock. The PDP lost the presidential vote to Muhammadu Buhari and the newly formed All Progressives Congress (APC) - a coalition of opposition parties and disgruntled former members. Thrust into the political wilderness the party's national leaders were bewildered - familiar with the trappings of federal power they had to work out what to do in opposition. This was the beginning of the end, according to political analyst Ishaq Buhari. "They were a party that was so used to power, being in opposition was a new challenge they struggled with from the start," he told the BBC. If 2015 was a major blow, 2025 was the year the party's foundations were left in ruins. It was marked by a dizzying wave of defections and bitter internal conflicts. A group of state governors switched party allegiance, which had a particularly devastating effect. At the start of that year, the PDP still held eight states. But by December, five state governors - from Delta, Akwa Ibom, Enugu, Bayelsa and Rivers - had gone over to the ruling APC. They cited the PDP's declining viability and a desire for better co-operation with the federal government as reasons for their departure. Early this year, the PDP held three states but that is now down to zero - with the Oyo governorship slipping from the party's hands just last month. Internal power struggles, factionalism, insistence that power rotates through the regions and disciplinary measures have all added to the sense of disillusionment within the party. The PDP has been robbed of high-profile figures and talent, including the loss of former Vice-President Atiku Aubakar last year. The crisis was intensified by a debilitating leadership tussle. In November 2025, a faction of the party, which observers say represented the majority of members, held a contentious national convention in Ibadan, Oyo state, despite court orders attempting to stop it. The convention expelled Nyesom Wike, a prominent PDP member who is serving in President Bola Tinubu's APC-led government. Wike, who helped found the party, heads a rival faction creating a political stand-off that has paralysed the PDP. He had controversially helped the APC win Rivers state in the last presidential election leading to accusations that he had betrayed the PDP. But in the eyes of the law the faction that he heads is the legitimate party. This means that it has been able to submit its slate of presidential and parliamentary candidates to the electoral commission leaving the rival faction without any representatives on the ballot. Despite the chaos, some die-hard loyalists remain optimistic. Politician and staunch PDP member Aminu Adamu, part of the anti-Wike faction, believes a return to its former glory is possible. He cites examples from Thailand and Argentina, where parties have bounced back after years in the wilderness. "We have seen it happen before," he tells the BBC. "All we need to do is put our house in order and start to build from there. "If we make all the necessary corrections, by 2032 I really think PDP can be a major force again." Others point out that the party still has a grassroots network - essential to win and sustain power - with offices, activists, supporters and local leaders. But by 2032 it may be too late. With the party in such disarray and candidates backed by Wike on the ballot - voters are unlikely to trust them. Analyst Deji Olarenwaju believes the only thing that could save the once-mighty party is an alliance with the African Democratic Congress - now seen as the biggest opposition group or Peter Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress. "Because on their own they are going nowhere," he says. item.title: Captured Ukrainian-born soldiers tell BBC why they fought for Russia
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn9nr195drzo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Captured Ukrainian-born soldiers tell BBC why they fought for Russia - Published In Western Ukraine, behind high walls and layers of locked gates, there is a camp full of men captured fighting for Russia. Many of those crouching in the shade around the edges of the prison yard were recruited from big cities like St Petersburg and Yekaterinburg, not far-flung and poorer regions like at the start of the full-scale invasion. But not all the prisoners are Russian. Amongst them are soldiers from Ukraine itself: the men who went to war with their own country. Interviewing prisoners of war is not straightforward: to be sure they are not being coerced, first and foremost, and then to assess how openly they are speaking in the circumstances. But with no access to the military inside Russia, it is a chance to assess the dynamics of this war and explore what might motivate the men fighting it. That includes the Ukrainian-born soldiers, on Russia's side. We gave everyone the right to refuse an interview and spoke to those who agreed far away from any guards, and without cameras. As well as several formal interviews, I was able to talk to prisoners directly, in Russian, in several locations. Anton was 10 when his part of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region was taken over by forces loyal to Moscow. In 2022, when Vladimir Putin escalated to all-out war, he turned 18 and signed up to fight immediately - for Russia. "I don't regret my choice. I went to defend my land," Anton insists and tells me his friends volunteered, too. "Then you get the SMS messages. Dead, dead, dead." Other prisoners say the same: that all those they went to war with have been killed. They also say fewer people are volunteering to replace them, despite enormous sign-up fees, which suggests Putin's desire to avoid mass mobilisation could soon be tested. When Ukraine captures its own citizens on the battlefield, they are put on trial for treason. But the men are then sent to PoW camps along with the Russians. Officially, Kyiv still sees them as Ukrainian and treats Russia's control of their regions as temporary. But the reality on the ground is more complex. "They're very pro-Russian, and their national identity is very blurred," is how Petro Yatsenko from Ukraine's coordination headquarters for PoWs puts it. Anton certainly does not class himself as a traitor. "I consider myself Russian. A country means nothing, it's all about nationality. All my family are from Russia. All my roots are from there," he says. When we wonder about his Ukrainian surname, he brushes that off as irrelevant. An entire generation born in Ukraine has now grown up under occupation, with Russian schooling and media fully controlled by the Kremlin. Both have portrayed the authorities in Kyiv as "Nazis" and illegitimate for many years. Since the full-scale invasion, even more territory has been subjected to the same. Anton has absorbed it all and now speaks almost entirely in Russian slogans. He calls Putin "my President" and thinks he should push to take the rest of the Donbas, even though hundreds of thousands have already been killed trying. "It's a shame that people died, especially those who are innocent," Anton says. "But war is war. It could have been ended. But no-one wanted to do that." In the prison hospital, Artyom lies in a corner bed, his body full of shrapnel. He had only been fighting for two months. From Donetsk, like Anton, he also went to war willingly - not just for the cash. "We have our own grudges," Artyom says, recalling how his region came under heavy fire in 2014 as Ukrainian forces tried to stop it breaking away from Kyiv. But his military experience has left him bitter. His commander was "bad" and he never got any of his 400,000 rouble (£3,470; $5,000) sign-up fee. To add insult to Artyom's many injuries, the wounded Russian soldier in the bed opposite was paid five times as much. All the Ukrainian-born PoWs we interviewed came from areas occupied since 2014 and almost all joined the Russian army voluntarily. But one man from Donetsk region told us he had been forced to fight. His eyes darted around as he talked, unsure who he could trust. One official tally, citing "intelligence", suggests more than 50,000 Ukrainians have been conscripted against their will in occupied areas. Others put the figure far higher. This man told us that when the Russians invaded, his family had stayed, not through any political or national allegiance but because Donetsk was their home. Now, his only ambition was to get back to his wife and children, then avoid being returned to the front. "I'm just going to hide," he confided. Beneath the hospital windows and newly whitewashed walls there are rows of strawberries and cucumbers planted by the prisoners. Further on, the stench of varnish from an outhouse is overpowering. An official lifts a gold-coloured plastic handle from a bag near the door. "Guess what this is for?" he challenges us, grinning. Inside, I do a double-take: the men working are hammering together wooden coffins. I am told the last contract the prison got was for garden sheds. This one feels macabre. Across the courtyard in another workshop a handful of PoWs are making artificial Christmas trees, gaudy baubles strung from their machines. Like the coffin-makers, they tell me they use their wages to buy extra food and cigarettes. Sergei was born in the Ukrainian city of Luhansk but says he is Russian like his parents, who moved to the Donbas when both countries were part of the Soviet Union. He joined the Russian army a decade ago "to defend my homeland", but claims he will retire when he gets back, not return to the front. "I've done my bit." Most will have no choice. Stacking plastic branches next to Sergei is a drug dealer who signed up, like many, "exclusively" to avoid a long jail term. "For me, 15 years in prison was too much," Konstantin explains. "I know it probably doesn't excuse me, but it's a fact. I'm 44 now, I would be 60. So no." But Vshniki, or convict-soldiers, have to survive to the end of the war to be released and in the assault troops the odds are not good. Three convicted murderers told us they had thought they could walk free after fighting for a year, only to have their contracts renewed automatically. When I ask about killing their fellow countrymen on the battlefield, Sergei calls the question "provocative" and does not want to answer. "I see nothing good in any war, and in a war like this there can be nothing good a priori," Konstantin replies carefully. "I'm not saying we're the same as Ukrainians, but we are close. We all have relatives there. This just isn't good." He still thinks his decision to fight was right. Neither he nor Sergei expect the war to end soon. Both believe Putin won't stop until he controls the whole Donbas. "But everyone I know there has had enough," Konstantin says. "I just want this to be over, as soon as possible." At lunchtime, the prisoners in navy overalls file into the dining hall with heads bowed and hands clasped behind their backs. As they eat - soup and stew - a video called Myths about Crimea plays on a loop, demolishing Russia's claim to historic ownership of the peninsula that it stole from Ukraine in 2014, but no-one pays the slightest attention. The re-education efforts feels half-hearted. For Kyiv, the real focus is on using these PoWs as swaps to bring its own soldiers home. But when it comes to negotiating exchange lists, it turns out the men from the Donbas are a low priority for Russia. "Only a dozen or so have been transferred this year," Konstantin complains. "It seems like they don't want to exchange us. I think we will be the last to go." item.title: Key Trump aide Natalie Harp suddenly in spotlight after years behind scenes
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c80nzdjgmk3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Key Trump aide Natalie Harp suddenly in spotlight after years behind scenes - Published Few people in US President Donald Trump's orbit have appeared as frequently by his side as Natalie Harp in recent years. One of Trump's longest-serving and most loyal aides, the 35-year-old is trusted with typing out his Truth Social posts, among other top responsibilities. She was thrust again into the spotlight this week by Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff - a Democrat and frequent Trump foil - when he name-checked her during a speech that has since gone viral. Ossoff attacked Trump's "travel with Natalie on their apparently defenceless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar". He was referring to the new Air Force One plane, as well as to reports that Harp joined Trump - and a small group of people - when he secretly swapped planes leaving Turkey last month. Here is what you need to know about the Trump assistant who has been called both a "gatekeeper" and a "comfort blanket". Following an unorthodox path to the White House A California native and member of a conservative Christian family, Harp followed an unorthodox path into an already unconventional White House. She rose to fame by crediting Trump with saving her life. In his first term, Trump got the Right to Try Act passed to give some patients greater access to experimental treatments, which Harp used for her bone cancer. She quickly gained prominence and popularity in Trump's Maga (Make America Great Again) wing of the Republican Party by talking about the experience, and soon after joined an advisory board for Trump's 2020 re-election campaign. "When I failed the chemotherapies that were on the market, no-one wanted me in their clinical trials," she said at the 2020 Republican National Convention. "They didn't give me the right to try experimental treatments. Mr President, you did, and without you, I'd have died waiting for them to be approved." After the event, Trump said: "She lit up the television screen like very few people I have ever seen do it." Following Trump's loss in that election, Harp found work hosting a show at the conservative One America News Network, or OAN. There, she became known as a ferocious Trump defender and promoter of false claims that he won the 2020 election. She left the network in 2022 to join Trump's next presidential campaign. Most accounts of Trump's views of Harp come via anonymous second-hand sources in books by reporters such as Maggie Haberman, Jonathan Swan or Michael Wolff, and very little is publicly known about her private life. "Trump is like everything that my mum taught us to respect," her brother Preston Harp said during a CNN, external interview on Tuesday. "So I think that's where her infatuation for Trump comes from, honestly." He added that Harp was fixated on the White House from a young age and had written letters to previous presidents, including George W Bush, during the Iraq war. He told CNN her "dream came true finally" when she got to the White House and that his sister was Trump's "biggest fan, so that's probably why he likes her". "And she's good looking, she's got a good personality. She thinks that he saved her life, so somebody living with that kind of gratitude must feel pretty good," he said. Harp's official title at the White House is executive assistant to the president, which typically denotes a lower-tier position that entails managing logistics, scheduling, communications flow and mundane - but vital - secretarial work. By all accounts, though, Harp has given the role new meaning and her profile is significantly higher than that of her predecessors, such as Madeleine Westerhout in Trump's first administration. How influential is Harp? When a CNN reporter earlier this week asked Trump about Ossoff's comments, the White House reacted angrily later on its official X account, saying the reporter, Kristen Holmes, had taken a "cheap shot" at a staff member. "Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question," another post directed at Holmes read. "They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive." Harp's presence as a staffer is nearly constant in Trump's second term. Reporters at the White House frequently see her standing just feet away from Trump in the Oval Office or boarding Air Force One for many of his domestic and international trips. "She's always around," one source close to the White House told the BBC. "Literally, always." Among White House insiders and members of the press, she is often referred to as the "human printer" because she is often spotted carrying a portable printer to provide Trump with hard copies of articles and social media posts, which he prefers. In practice, this means that Harp has an outsized ability to control what information or updates Trump receives, according to another source familiar with White House operations. Other anonymous sources have described her to US media outlets as a "gatekeeper" and "comfort blanket". Harp also serves as something of a social media scribe for Trump, posting to his Truth Social account on his behalf. In one image that has been widely shared in the aftermath of Ossoff's comments, Harp is shown typing a post - in the president's own writing style - as he dictates to her while watching a speech by Kamala Harris in 2024. Amid the recent focus on Harp, the White House has described her as a "trusted and valued" member of the team, although Trump has rarely spoken about her on camera. Ossoff was one of many Trump critics who noted Harp was reportedly on the plane that the president boarded to leave Turkey after the US supposedly received information about a threat from Iran. Reporter Haberman, who has also reported extensively on Trump's presidencies, was asked during an appearance on the news network MSNOW why Trump took Harp with him on the secret plane: "Because she is sort of his binky, for lack of a better way of putting it, a comfort blanket." Haberman and Swan reported for the New York Times in 2024 that Harp had supposedly written in a letter to Trump: "You are all that matters to me."

item.title: Trial of mum accused of killing her three children puts postpartum psychosis on the map
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yedy98j7po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Lindsay Clancy's trial puts postpartum psychosis in the spotlight - Published Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide A month before Lindsay Clancy killed her three children, she went to her mother and then-husband and told them she had "thoughts of harming the children". Clancy's mother Paula Musgrove testified this week that during that time Lindsay would say: "'This isn't me, I've never been like this before.' And I would agree, because she wasn't." Clancy is not disputing that she carried out the killings, but has pleaded not guilty to murder charges. Her defence argues that Clancy was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she took her children's lives. Her symptoms included hallucinations and delusions that began after the birth of her third child. "She was unable to conform her behaviour to the rule of law and she had no appreciation for the wrongfulness of her act," Paul Zeizel, a clinical and forensic psychologist, said on the stand on Wednesday. Prosecutors, meanwhile, alleged she made a calculated decision to intentionally kill her children - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months. With postpartum psychosis, a rare condition that is considered a medical emergency, patients can experience mania, depression or a mixture of both. They also endure psychotic symptoms, such as hearing voices that aren't there. In uncommon, severe cases, they may harm or kill themselves or other people. It is among the most serious illnesses a woman can experience after giving birth, experts told the BBC, but it remains unclassified in medicine's encyclopaedia of psychiatry. The illness is gaining more attention as Clancy's trial approaches the one-month mark, and has opened up a dialogue about the mental health complications that women can experience after giving birth. What is postpartum psychosis? Postpartum psychosis often presents with mood symptoms such as irritability, mood swings, insomnia and what medical professionals would call a delirium-like state, Susan Hatters-Friedman, forensic psychiatry professor at Case Western Reserve University, told the BBC. "Psychosis in general as a term means that the person's out of touch with reality, and that often includes hallucinations, hearing things, seeing things that aren't there, delusions, which are fixed false beliefs that are not consistent with your culture," Hatters-Friedman said. Meghan Cliffel was eight months postpartum from the birth of her second daughter when she lost touch with reality. It was a Friday in 2015 and she had just finished her workday in New York City. She became convinced that people were following her, she thought she was being recruited for a cult, and she thought the world - including her husband - was out to get her and her two daughters. Some 24 hours later, she was handcuffed to a gurney and taken to a psychiatric hospital. She would go on to spend the next 12 days there receiving treatment for postpartum psychosis. Psychiatric symptoms, like the ones Cliffel experienced, can appear rapidly, Hatters-Friedman said. That is why it needs to be treated as a medical emergency, experts say. A person can be fine and then suddenly lose touch with reality. On the day Clancy killed her children, she played with them outside building a snowman, her former husband, Patrick Clancy, said. "She was having one of her best days," he told the court during the trial. Clancy had previously told her then-husband she was having thoughts of suicide or harming the children, but on that day everything seemed better, he testified. When evening came that January 2023, he went out to grab dinner for the family of five. When he returned, he found his children dead and Clancy injured from a suicide attempt. That contrast demonstrates the light-switch - or waxing and waning effect - that can be postpartum psychosis, experts told the BBC. "A woman can appear fine one minute and be really ill a little bit later," said Jennifer Payne, a reproductive psychiatry expert at the University of Virginia. Experts say it's not entirely clear what causes postpartum psychosis. It could be related to hormonal changes and stress after giving birth, and there seems to be a link between previous mental health challenges and developing the illness while postpartum. Recognition in the DSM-5 There is one major barrier standing in the way of awareness and better treatment of postpartum psychosis, experts and Cliffel agreed - it needs to be formally included in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, commonly referred to as the DSM-5. It's the mental health handbook published by the American Psychiatric Association. Veerle Bergink, a professor of psychiatry and the director of the Mount Sinai Women's Mental Health Center, is among the people working diligently to get postpartum psychosis included in the DSM-5. Without a mention there, the illness does not get discussed in medical school textbooks; students do not learn about it, and people do not talk about it much. Its addition is essential, she said. "You can only investigate and talk about the disease if you give the disease a name, and if it has criteria," Bergink said. "So you don't get research funded, there is no money, there is no care system, there is no insurance code." For people like Cliffel, who experienced the illness first-hand, the lack of mention in the DSM-5 is "bananas". "It feels like an erasure," she said. "I know how healing it is to have somebody finally name what you have." She too referenced the cascading effects that the lack of classification has on educating clinicians, family knowledge and insurance coverage. "And so I see this moment," she said, referencing the Clancy trial, "[as one where] we cannot be surprised when tragedy happens, and instead, we can proactively build to care for mothers and families." What does treatment look like? Postpartum psychosis is treatable, experts stressed. Lithium, a mood stabiliser, is a common way to treat the illness. It is often given to patients to prevent a relapse. But a variety of other treatments - including electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) and antipsychotic medications - are also used depending on the patient and their symptoms. Many women will require a stay in a psychiatric hospital, Hatters-Friedman said, but with treatment people can recover. The outcome in Clancy's story is a very rare one, experts said. Women with postpartum psychosis hurt or kill children between 1% and 4% of the time, research shows, external. For Cliffel, her treatment plan had many prongs. She went to therapy, did Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) therapy (a type of psychotherapy), and took lithium for a full year. Much of the treatment that helped her, she found by happenstance. "There wasn't a ladder of care [showing] 'this is how you heal from this experience'," Cliffel said. She recalled speaking with breast cancer survivors who told her there were clear steps to follow after a breast cancer diagnosis. "It's not like that for postpartum psychosis, so it was a lot of kind of like fumbling around in the dark," Cliffel said. But medical professionals gave her tools and the treatment she needed to go on and have a third child. To ensure she did not experience postpartum psychosis again, as soon as her son was born, she began taking lithium, and did so for a full year after his birth. "We should have a system that actually understands maternal mental health and gives proactive support to all parents and educates them about the things that can happen," she said. "I mean, maternal mental health issues are the most common complication of childbirth." Related topics - Published1 day ago

Why is Ukraine's ex-defence minister calling for wartime elections? Ukraine's popular ex-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for wartime elections, in what has been seen as a major challenge to President Volodymyr Zelensky. The country has been under martial law since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, meaning elections have been suspended. "Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia," Fedorov said in a video posted on Tuesday. But there are practical concerns as to how free and fair elections could be held in a war-torn nation, which Fedorov has not addressed. Fedorov has also not confirmed if he would run against Zelensky. The BBC's Dan Johnson reports from Kyiv.
